item.title: Claude Code real-device E2E: 31 fixes in 3 rounds – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Claude Code real-device E2E: 31 fixes in 3 rounds

We ran a Flutter app that Claude Code had built through three rounds of end-to-end tests on a real phone and an emulator. Unit tests passed at the end of every round, and we still fixed 31 defects.

The first button on the first screen did nothing. That was the start of a morning spent walking a Flutter family app through sign-up, invites, AI suggestions and account deletion on a Galaxy S21 and a PC emulator, with its unit tests passing. A Claude Code agent had committed the zero-cost test stack minutes earlier; three rounds later, 31 defects had been fixed.

Every unit test was green, which is when an agent reports it is done. The guard that kept the test build away from production was wrong at first: a test build documented as running "without the real cloud" sent requests to Google servers every time it ran, until October 13. Requests that the Firebase SDK opens on its own do not go through the local emulator connection.

07:53: the Start button did nothing on either device

At 07:37 KST on October 10, 2026, Claude Code committed a local test stack for the family calendar app AXFamily and went straight into device E2E (end-to-end testing: using the whole app in the order a person would). Device A was the operator's own Galaxy S21; device B was an Android emulator on the PC.

When Start did nothing, the agent dumped the view hierarchy, read the router, and wrote a failing test before touching the code. The router's navigation rule should have sent a user in onboarding to the age check, but that step listed the welcome screen as an allowed route, so the rule sent them nowhere.

Sign-up then failed on both devices. The app pointed at the local Firebase stack on 127.0.0.1, but FlutterFire, the Firebase plugin set for Flutter, rewrites that address to 10.0.2.2 by default. Both devices failed with 'Cleartext HTTP traffic to 10.0.2.2 not permitted', because the test build allowed plain HTTP only to 127.0.0.1 and localhost. And 10.0.2.2 reaches the host PC only from inside an emulator, so even with that allowed the S21 could not have reached it.

Creating a family failed next: every server function call broke because the fake API key was not in the format Firebase expects. Each fix meant rebuilding the release APK with R8 (Android's code shrinker for release builds) and reinstalling it. The first build took about five and a half minutes and later rebuilds mostly one to three.

The zero-cost stack swapped four services for fakes

Commit 1fcc1e1 swapped four real services for local stand-ins:

Real serviceStand-inCondition that keeps it out of production
Firebase Auth, Firestore, FunctionsFirebase Local Emulator Suite on the PCOnly projects whose ID starts with demo- (they have no real resources)
AI extraction modelA deterministic fake modelOnly when the Functions emulator flag and a demo- project are both true
Photo storage serverA local photo server (a Worker) on the PCLocal config and a demo- project
App Check (app attestation)An unsigned local tokenOnly the emulator accepts it; production functions take signed tokens only

Firebase's own debug App Check provider was an option, but it has to exchange tokens with Google's servers, which a demo- project cannot do.

The other direction is guarded too. The release gate opens the production AAB and searches the compiled code (dex) and the Flutter code library (libapp.so) for test marker strings; any hit stops the release. A CI check confirms the guard statements are still in the source and that a copy with each guard deleted fails the check. The harness commit shipped 14 of these guard-removal cases. Why a gate should read the artifact itself is in Our release gates were checking something other than the release.

Unit tests were green after every round

RoundTime (KST)R8 APK builds
107:44-09:489
209:48-11:012
311:01-12:254

Each round ran Android's monkey tool for 3,000 random events on both devices with no crashes or ANRs (app-not-responding errors). The instructions asked the agent to look for R8 symptoms in the logs, classes or methods the shrinker had removed, and there were none. The case where R8 did kill a release build, in a different app, is in AI-built Android app release checklist: R8 and real devices.

What showed up instead were flow and state defects. After B joined the family, A could not assign a task to B until A restarted the app, a defect you only see when two accounts take turns; after an AI suggestion was approved, the Today screen stayed on the first-run card because the app never heard about the server's write. The round 1 and round 3 commit messages say each of their 18 fixes came with a test that fails without the fix. When the harness was committed, all 1,118 Flutter tests passed with the round 1 defects still in the code.

One round 3 fix: on device B, AI organizing ended with a retryable error, yet the banner at the top of the Records tab kept saying a result was waiting. It had been left open in round 2; round 3 marked the pending record as failed and changed the text.

We also counted whether any defect appeared only on the real phone. None of the fix records says "S21 only". One defect surfaced because of the emulator: it ran on GMT while the S21 used Seoul time, the same as the family, so a date picker whose "today" followed the device time zone looked wrong only on the emulator.

"Without the real cloud" was false until October 13

The harness README opened by saying it runs the core flow on two devices without the real cloud. Round 1's report already contradicted it: a Google logging endpoint answered with HTTP 200 and Firebase Installations (the service that issues an ID per install) rejected requests with HTTP 400, so requests were leaving the device. The agent noted in its own report that the 400s started after it fixed the fake key's format.

At the end of round 3 each app process still logged 24 Installations warnings. That afternoon, commit 753cc37 switched off Firebase's automatic collection settings in the test build and the README said there were no Installations or FCM registration requests. Thirty-five minutes later a review fix, c2aeb59, noted that only one setting had actually changed and downgraded the line: until a device showed zero requests, "network zero" was not done.

The next day a QA run on the operator's other phone, a Galaxy S20, logged the Installations 400 again and settled that open item as false. The cause it named was a push token request.

The harness redirected only the server addresses the app calls itself; requests the SDKs open on their own were outside it. And the isolation gate read source statements and strings inside the artifact, so the harness commit's 21 isolation tests checked network config such as the cleartext host list, but none blocked or counted a running app's outbound connections.

On October 13, commit d90e21a blocked traffic at the transport layer instead of switching off more settings:

  • An empty ContentProvider (an Android component created at app start, before Firebase) replaces Java's https handler with one that always refuses.
  • The test build's network security config (NSC) trusts zero certificates, so any other TLS connection fails at the handshake.
  • Dart's HttpClient may open only local plain-http connections.

The same day a device script counted the off-device bytes of the app's UID (the user number Android gives each app): zero on both the S21 and the S20. Review then pointed out that a zero alone cannot be told apart from a broken counter that always returns zero, so a PASS now also requires the system UID, counted the same way, to be above zero.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The day we stopped using the emulator

At 14:32 on October 11 the operator asked why the agent kept starting the PC emulator when it had been told to test on the S20. The agent shut the emulator down and said it had itself told the store-screenshot agent to use it. Commit 9fcff82 that afternoon traced the root cause to an old decision in the plan, "Second test device: Play image emulator. Do not use the S20.", plus two lines in its table that echoed it.

The old decision is now struck through, with a new one beneath it: S21 is device A, S20 is device B. The install script exits, with no override, when the device serial starts with emulator- or the system properties say it is one, and a docs check fails if the three old sentences come back. The GMT device that caught the time zone defect went with it.

Building the same harness

Accept an agent's "done" only when it comes with a round record of the release build run end to end on two devices. Here is how to get that record without paying for cloud time.

  1. Build the test APK with production's release and R8 settings, and let one build constant (a dart-define) pull in the test code. Add a package suffix, debug-key-only signing and a ban on Play bundles (AABs).

  2. Choose the fake backend and fake model only when "running in the emulator" and "demo- project" are both true; if only one is, refuse the call.

  3. Turn off FlutterFire's host rewriting and connect with adb reverse, which forwards a PC port to 127.0.0.1 on the device. Allow cleartext only for 127.0.0.1 and localhost.

    firestore.useFirestoreEmulator('127.0.0.1', 8180, automaticHostMapping: false);
adb -s <device> reverse tcp:8180 tcp:8180

  4. Have the release gate search the production AAB for test markers, and lock it with guard-removal cases that must fail.

  5. Give the two devices different languages and time zones and run a 12-step scenario covering sign-up, invites, AI suggestions, photos and account deletion. For each defect: failing test, fix, rebuild the APK, recheck on the device.

  6. Count off-device traffic on the device from dumpsys netstats detail by the app's UID. The increase must be zero, the blocker's install log must be present, and the system UID, counted the same way, must be above zero. That output also holds other apps and carrier identifiers, so filter on the device and pull out only the numbers.

  7. Make the install script refuse devices you have decided not to use.

Errors we hit

SymptomCauseFix
Sign-up fails with Cleartext HTTP traffic to 10.0.2.2 not permittedFlutterFire's automatic host mappingautomaticHostMapping: false
Every server function call (callable) throws IllegalArgumentException (valid API key)The fake key did not match the Installations format (39 characters starting with A)A fake key in the right format
Firestore triggers die with default Firebase app does not existA check that skipped default app setupCheck for the default app (the bug was in production too)

Purchases, push and Play Integrity went to a separate runbook

Completed Play purchases, real push delivery, photo file deletion and App Check tokens backed by Play Integrity (Google's check that the app came from Play) are out of reach for this harness. Device tests with the real AI model and production backend got their own runbook on October 13 and install through Play's internal testing track. The same day the operator set the bar: the E2E has to pass clearly on the S20 and S21 before anything counts as done.

The Firebase emulator produced its own errors. Family deletion failed several times with CANCELLED; the agent put that down to the emulator but added retries anyway. Whether production Firestore does the same is something this harness cannot show.

With a personal phone as device A, the agent kept the share sheet and photo picker closed, because they show contacts and personal photos. Photo steps ran on device B, and round 3 recorded the invite-code hand-off as a partial pass caused by the harness.

The round 3 fix to the account deletion screen could not be reproduced on a device again and is covered only by unit and widget tests. A checklist step that sets one phone to a time zone different from the family's is what would catch the date picker class of defect again; this project's checklist has no such step today.

Questions or ideas?

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Is passing on the emulator enough to ship?

Not on this record. None of the 31 defects was marked as real-phone only, but a library default that assumes an emulator blocked both devices and pointed the real phone at an address it could never reach, and the time zone difference between the two devices exposed a defect.

How do I connect a Flutter release build to the Firebase Local Emulator Suite?

Apps targeting Android 9 or later block cleartext HTTP by default. Allow cleartext only for 127.0.0.1 in the test build's network security config, then connect with automaticHostMapping: false and adb reverse.

item.title: Claude Code fix: Naver spelling highlights missing – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Claude Code fix: Naver spelling highlights missing

The missing highlights were errors at the end of a sentence. A request tag the server folded into the correction and a strict length check each dropped them; after fixing both with Claude Code, all 31 errors in the saved responses get colour.

Type "이거 어떻해" (a common misspelling of "what do I do") into the SugarSpeller app and it used to show no highlight at all. The chat-style screen went further and told the user there were no spelling errors. Naver, the Korean portal whose spell checker the app calls, was returning the right correction the whole time. Replaying the colouring logic from before the September 13, 2026 fix on saved server responses, only 17 of the 31 errors Naver flagged got colour.

Every one of the 14 misses was the last error in its sentence. The causes were a string appended to the request body and one comparison that filters out ranges reaching the end. If your app paints corrections from an external spelling or translation service, look at those two places first.

Short sentences came back with no colour at all

The app has two screens: Chat, which shows results as message bubbles, and the older Classic screen with separate input and output boxes. At 18:14 KST on September 13, 2026, the operator asked Claude Code to investigate: highlighting did nothing in Chat and was unreliable in Classic, and Naver should be analysed first.

The agent's first suspect was the response parser. It fetched live Naver responses and ran them through the app's regular expression; every corrected word and error type came out correctly, so parsing was ruled out. Its second suspect was how Classic matches each response to its chunk (long input is split into chunks). Ten measured sentences produced zero mismatches.

At 18:27 the agent tested what it called its last hypothesis: a short sentence whose only error is at the end. The result came a minute later: of 10 short sentences, Naver found errors in 7, and all 7 got zero colour. The pair below is that case as it was later saved in the repository's test data.

A tag and an operator erased the same error

To tell which chunk a response belonged to, the app appended a tag (in Chat, the message's unique ID and chunk number; in Classic, the chunk number and a hash of the sentence) to the text it sent. Naver read the tag as part of the last word and returned it inside the em element that marks the corrected span.

The app stripped the tag only from the corrected sentence it displays. The list of corrected words still held "어떡해-…-0", so indexOf, which looks up the word's position in the displayed sentence, returned -1 (not found), and an error the app can't locate gets no colour.

Chat counted the corrected words it managed to find on screen, and when that count was zero it said "no spelling errors". Classic used Naver's own error count field, errata_count, so it reported the right number and showed no colour.

The second defect had nothing to do with the tag. Colour was applied only when buffer.length > key + text.length: the displayed sentence had to be longer than the word's start position (key) plus the word's length (text.length), meaning the range had to end before the last character. "이거 어떡해" is 6 characters and the corrected word ends at character 6, so 6 > 6 is false and nothing was painted. A short sentence often has one error, at the end, which leaves the screen with no colour.

Because both defects remove the same error, fixing one barely helps.

Both defects predate any AI-co-authored commit in the repository. Appending an identifier to the request text (then a hash of the sentence) first appeared in December 2020, in the original screen that later became Classic (6baa0ae).

The comparison came in April 2021 with commit 3ad9ba4, titled as a fix for an IndexOutOfBoundsException in the colour-span call. A guard written to stop an out-of-range crash also blocked ranges that end exactly at the end.

In August 2025, when Chat was rebuilt with Claude Code, two commits (02cbb15 and 5f082f8) copied both habits into the new screen: the new request code appended the tag, and the new colouring loop used the same comparison.

Start with a short sentence whose only error is the last word

  1. Check a short sentence whose only error is the last word. If nothing is highlighted, look at the next two places.

  2. In the request builder, look for an order number, hash or UUID appended to the text being checked. Move it into the HTTP client's request tag or the callback closure.

  3. Find the range check right before colouring. If it reads length > end or end < length, it should be end <= length. The grep below only finds the length > start + length form this app had; check length > end, end < length and Java's length() separately.

    grep -rnE '(length|size) *> *[a-z]+ *\+' app/src/main

  4. Save real responses as test data files. Assert that the error-count field equals the number of coloured ranges, that each range's substring equals the corrected word, and that ranges don't overlap.

  5. Revert the fixed line for a moment and confirm the tests fail. If they still pass, they won't catch the bug when it comes back.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The 26/26 check was never in the repository

At 20:41 the agent committed e9cd771, fixing both defects and Chat's error count, and reported that a live cross-check on 18 sentences now coloured every error. The report also listed the number of passing unit tests.

At 22:13 the operator asked whether the Naver tests were all committed. The agent replied that only 10 pure-logic tests were in the commit; the live cross-check depended on response files in a scratch folder and had been deleted as a one-off.

Eleven minutes later commit 9ed4dca landed. It stores verbatim server responses in the repository as a fixture (fixed test data): 23 sentences sent without the tag, and the same sentences sent the old way with the tag attached. A mutation check, temporarily reverting the fix, showed 9 tests failing when end-of-string ranges are dropped again.

NumberWhat it countsRecord
7 of 7 with no colourfirst analysis, 7 of 10 short sentences that had errorssession log, 18:28
16 of 26, then 26one-off check on 18 sentences, not in the repositorycommit e9cd771 message
17 of 31, then 3123 fixture pairs; sentences with no colour went from 9 to 0commit 9ed4dca test

On November 16, 2026, a Python port of the same comparison run over this fixture gave 17 of 31 again. All nine zero-colour sentences have a single error, in the last word: five were written for exactly that case, and the other four mix in a line break, a long number, a Latin word or a trailing space.

The chunk number now rides in the request tag

Never put identifiers into the body you send to an external API. The app now carries the chunk number in the OkHttp request tag, a value that never leaves the device and comes back with the response callback. It dropped the old approach of stripping the tag from the response with regular expressions: those patterns could also delete a user's 13-digit numbers or long Latin words, which is what the long-number and Latin-word sentences in the chart contain.

What changedPrevious behaviour, and why it went
a range that ends at the last character is colouredthe old comparison; the final error was always dropped
a word that isn't found is skipped and the search position keptthe position was left at -1; the next word was searched from the start and colour landed in the wrong place
both screens count errors with errata_countcount of words found; a miss turned into "no errors"
one shared colouring class (SpellHighlighter)three copies (Chat, Classic, Daum); fixing one let the others drift

The same evening the Daum checker (another Korean portal) turned out to be failing outright; that story is in Daum spell check failed: OkHttp and a JS redirect.

The fixture is one day of responses

If Naver changes its response format, the offline tests keep passing while the app breaks again, and since this is not a public API there is no notice of such changes.

No response seen so far has put a line break or a character like < inside a correction span. The current code turns < back into < only in the displayed sentence, so such a response would leave < in the corrected word and < on screen, and the word would not be found. The mobile responses have only ever used two error types (spacing and spelling); the colours for the other two are untested against real data.

Still to check: fetch the same 23 sentences from the live server and compare the format with the fixture, and look for a sentence that puts a special character inside a correction span.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why does only the last word miss its highlight in Naver spell check results?

In this app there were two causes. A tag appended to the request ended up inside the last correction span, so the word could not be located, and a comparison refused any range ending at the last character. Both only hit the error at the end of a sentence.

Can a SpannableString span end exactly at the string length?

Yes. The end index is exclusive, so an end equal to the length colours up to the last character. Only an end beyond the length throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

App repository git history (commits 6baa0ae, 3ad9ba4, 02cbb15, 5f082f8, e9cd771, 9ed4dca, 0b74357; the 2025-08 commits co-authored with Claude, the 2026-09 commits with Claude Opus 5), real-response fixtures (48 Naver lines, 28 Daum lines) and their cross-check tests, changelog section 1.6.017, Claude Code session log of 2026-09-13 (KST), project memory note on measured Naver responses (2026-09-13).

item.title: Claude Code handoff to a session that had stopped – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Short note

Claude Code handoff to a session that had stopped

Our Claude Code session handed work to the "dev session" its own docs named, but that session had stopped 25 hours before. We now write the owner, with a date, as one line in memory.

Six lines in three documents assigned work to "the other session" or "the dev session". On the afternoon of October 18, 2026, the Claude Code session running marketing for two of our Android games followed the rule line, said it would pass its day-one drop-off analysis to the dev session, and wrote four more dev-session lines into its drop-off report. The dev session's last record was a commit at 15:30 the day before.

At 16:52 the operator corrected it: there is no other dev session right now, and you own both games. Within three minutes the marketing session itself had built the test-device filter it had meant to ask the dev session for.

The plan line was written while the dev session ran

At 08:48 on October 17 the operator told the marketing session that another session was fixing the games from GA4 (Google Analytics 4) data, so it should stay on marketing. A dev session opened in the game repository had been working since 07:52 and committing fixes since 08:55. The plan document's third line, saying game fixes were being done by the other session, was written that morning. The operating rules that every scheduled run reads first also said "app code or build changes: the other session handles these."

At 15:29 the operator told the dev session, roughly, "commit, and another session will pick it up." It made commit 64267f2 and went quiet until October 22. Nothing the marketing session reads recorded that ending.

Not knowing that, the marketing session pointed at another session in 9 replies, 5 of them after the dev session had stopped. The last three came on October 18 between 16:27 and 16:41.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

A present-tense rule outlived its session

The marketing session kept following the rule line its 09:17 scheduled run on October 18 had read, "the other session handles these", 25 hours after that session stopped. The day-one drop-off report it wrote at 16:38 mentioned the dev session four times; one line asked the dev session to filter two test phones out of GA4. Those phones were the ones this same work used.

Ten seconds after the correction the agent said the earlier "dev session" was just an earlier part of this same work, then grepped the three documents and found the six lines.

Once the GA4 report tool dropped test and review devices by default, organic installs in Korea (installs not from ads) for Block Turn since October 11 went from 7 to 2; the rest were test devices. The session deleted the rule line and rewrote the four report lines as past facts, but it left the plan alone, and its third line is still there on November 17.

Ownership as one dated memory line

Don't hand work to a session by name. Find the lines in your plan and rule documents that point at a session, then check the last message time in that session's log (a per-project jsonl file).

grep -n "다른 세션\|개발 세션" *.md

If the session has stopped, rewrite the line as a past fact and write the owner into project memory, the notes file Claude Code reads when a session starts. Fixing document lines alone means hunting down every document already written, and it does nothing for the next one. This project's memory now says the "dev session" in older documents was "Claude's own work in an earlier conversation" and must not be handed anything, and the memory index (MEMORY.md) carries one line: no other session (10/18).

That line is false when sessions really do run in parallel. At 16:34 the same day the operator told a session in another app repository that search work (SEO and GEO) would be handled in a different session. For that case we write an owner for each file, as in Multiple Claude Code sessions: one owner per file.

The same misreading also ran the other way. When the operator reopened the October 17 dev conversation on October 22, it listed the marketing session's GA4 analysis and test-device filter from the 18th and said other sessions had carried the work on in the meantime. Next to check: whether two sessions worked in the game repository at the same time after that, and how the "no other session" line was read that day.

Checked 2026-11-17. Two Claude Code session logs (marketing Oct 9 to 21, dev Oct 15 to 30, 2026, times in KST), game repository git history (commits d1f6de1, 64267f2, 44c6acd), current copies of the three operating documents and the grep output from 2026-10-18, project memory (2026-10-18).

item.title: Claude Code re-review: the bug survived via HTTP – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Retrospective

Claude Code re-review: the bug survived via HTTP

We re-reviewed Claude Code's fixes four times, and the blocker-plus-high count never reached zero. The second pass found a defect the first fix had created; the third found a defect marked closed still open over HTTP.

We sent code fixed by Claude Code agents back through an adversarial review (a review that asks where the code breaks if someone attacks it), and the second pass found a defect the first fix had created; the third found that a defect recorded as closed was still alive through a different connection path. This was SugarMount's P2P chat app (Flutter), during release prep in September 2026, and we ran that review four times.

The second review's defect was where two fixes met; the third's was on an HTTP path the fix never touched and in server docs that promised something untrue. When the third defect turned up, the fix report, the server docs and the server tests all said it was closed.

The lobby lock, found and fixed within 69 minutes of the first fix

The first review (September 8) found 42 issues in the release-prep changes. Each finding carried a severity: Blocker (stops the release), High, Medium or Low, and both blockers were about identity. The app trusted whatever peer id (the identifier for a chat partner) the other side sent, and the signalling server (the lobby service that helps devices on a network find each other) let anyone join under someone else's id.

Five agents split the fix by file, and it landed as one commit at 00:36 on September 9. Ids are now computed from the public key and never change, and the server binds an id to its first claimer. Both were what the first review had proposed.

The second review was done by a separate agent that wrote a report and changed no code, reading that one commit. Put the two fixes together and a permanent id becomes a target: whoever claims it first shuts the real owner out, and the app treats that refusal as fatal and never reconnects, so the owner never shows up in the lobby again. The report noted that before the fix a second join had been allowed, so this lobby lock was a new defect. The round-two fix commit message calls the lock "introduced by the previous round".

The report's first item, forged message bubbles, had fallen between fixes as well. The agent that owned the history sync path had added checks on a message's room and sender, but the live message path belonged to another agent's files and got none. A connected peer could plant a bubble on the other user's screen that looked like their own message. The report called it an item that "fell at the boundary between two agents".

The new claim-expiry rule only covered WebSocket

The fix agent that took the server items (its report is named R8) limited a claim to the life of the connection plus a short grace period. Its report said a permanent lock was no longer possible, the server README and protocol doc said the same, and the server tests passed.

The third review read the 03:38 commit from a frozen copy made with git archive, because the working tree held other agents' uncommitted changes. This is what it put at the top of its "fix now" list. The review documents number their items: round two's start with RR-, round three's with TR-.

Clients reach the server over WebSocket, or over HTTP when WebSocket fails. The rule that lets a claim expire only applied to WebSocket connections. A peer registered over HTTP went down a different branch where the claim never expired, so HTTP requests alone, with no socket open, could keep an id held. A separate review track measured it: all 10 of the owner's WebSocket joins were refused.

It found the same shape in three more places:

  • The server gives an id's first claimer a join secret (the value that proves ownership when it comes back). The path that lets an app recover its id after a restart handed back the existing join secret, so passing a narrow check once was enough to hold that id from any address (TR-2).
  • The web build does not connect devices directly; it uses a relay transport through the server. The handshake change that stops us sending our hello (the first message after connecting, carrying the public key and nickname) to a blocked peer first never reached that transport. The relay transport did not implement the new interface, so it quietly kept the old behaviour.
  • Message timestamps travelled without a time zone, so two devices in different zones failed every hash check on each other's messages. Our two emulators ran on one PC in one zone and could not produce this (TR-26).

The third fix commit, at 10:10, is titled "close the paths the earlier fixes did not cover". HTTP claims now need the join secret, and the recovery path issues a fresh secret.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

We had treated a red guard as proof

The rule for this round was that every fix gets a test that fails when its guard is removed. The reviewers checked that claim themselves: round two reran 3 of the fix reports' guard-removal experiments and round three reran 8; every one went red when its guard was removed, and all but one (which failed one test more than reported) matched the reported counts and names. The HTTP lock was there anyway.

Removing a guard only tests the paths that have the guard. The HTTP path never had one to remove, and the third review's test-gap table says the HTTP lock "was never covered in the first place". On the restart path the tests protected the defect: a server test written by the fix agent asserted that a restarted app gets the same secret back, so TR-2 could not show up as a test failure.

Checking tests by deleting guards is covered in 3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database. The defects in this note are the ones still there after that check passed.

The server fix agent changed only the WebSocket path, then wrote the no-permanent-lock guarantee into its report and the server docs, backed by tests that covered only the path it had changed. An agent caught the defect too, and that reviewer had its own wrong hypothesis: the third reviewer suspected that a rejected hello kept the socket occupied, wrote a test on its copy, found the hypothesis wrong and recorded no defect. Its report gives the reason as running it "so as not to report a guess".

The records show a person's hand in one place, the rules: the operator's shared working instructions now say that after a large fix you run one more adversarial review, look for other paths to the same defect, and grep the number of production callers. Who asked for each rerun we could not confirm, because the session logs from that week are not on this PC.

When you review a fix commit, count whether its guard covers every entrance to the same defect before you ask whether the guard turns red.

Six axes for finding the other entrances

The third review concluded that uncovered paths had been where the defects were, again and again, and that the next round should ask whether each guard applies to every transport and path in production. Grouping the entrances the defects used across the four reviews gives six axes.

AxisWhat it caught in this appHow it was checked
TransportWebSocket fixed, HTTP open (TR-1); web relay without the new handshake (TR-8)Find every implementation of the interface and check each for the guard
Data pathRoom and sender checks on sync but not on live messages (RR-1)List every function that receives the same data and compare their checks
Reissue and recoveryRestart recovery returned the existing secret (TR-2)At every branch that hands out a secret or state, ask whether it makes a new one or copies the old
Doc guarantees"No id is held for good" in the server docs (TR-1); "no lower bound" in the design docs (round 4)Match each "never", "always" or "cannot" sentence against code and tests
CallersNickname masking registered nowhere (RR-5); older-history page API with no callers (TR-19)Grep production code for callers of every new API
EnvironmentZone-less timestamps that same-zone emulators cannot expose (TR-26)Write down conditions the test setup cannot create

The six axes come from this app's shape. Server connections go over WebSocket or HTTP and chat links over TCP or a web relay, which made the transport axis long. We have not used the list on an app with a single transport. Writing the environment axis in a table does not close it; the third review asked for a QA case with the two devices set to different time zones.

The caller axis is not unique to this app. A month later, a device E2E fix commit in AXFamily, our family scheduling app (October 10), notes that nothing passed received photos and PDFs on to the organising screen. That app's merge review is in Every branch passed its AI review, and the merged code still had 12 defects.

  1. For each fix commit, write the defect it blocks in one sentence: what comes in, through which entrance, and what it does.

  2. For each of the six axes, list the entrances that defect could use. Write "none" for an axis that does not apply.

  3. Grep each entrance for the same guard. The third review counted interface implementations, call sites of the limit check, and production callers of each new API. For this app:

    # every class implementing the interface the transports share
grep -rn "implements TransportService" lib/
# production callers of the API that reads older history page by page
grep -rn "getMessagesPage\|MessageCursor" lib/

  4. Give the fix diff to a review agent that took no part in the fix, report only, and have it mark each earlier finding closed, partial or open.

  5. Read the fix agent's tests that lock in current behaviour as correct. A test asserting that the same value comes back can lock in the defect too.

  6. Set the stop condition before you run the review. This app's last review brief set it as: open no new verification areas, fix only blockers and highs, move medium and below to the backlog.

Four rounds, never zero

No round found fewer than 18 issues (chart below), and the blocker-plus-high count never reached zero. Round two read a single fix commit (83 files), and its document has no tally line, so only findings tagged with a severity are counted.

Round four read the latest fix bundle and judged 24 of its 26 findings to be defects that bundle had introduced. Its brief cited the record that every earlier review had found new defects made by the previous fix, and set the stopping point in advance. We stopped on that rule instead of waiting for zero, and the 16 findings rated medium or lower were marked as backlog candidates.

Neither the fix reports' "closed" nor matching guard-removal results held up as proof of closure this time. The fix agents checked their own fixes with guard-removal runs, but there is no record of any of them reviewing its own fix adversarially, so there is nothing to compare.

Round two confirmed the lobby lock and the forged bubble by reading code only; reproducing them with two real clients was left for a later round. Nobody launched the web build to see the relay defect either. Defect reports can be wrong too: the round-four brief counts 5 reported defects withdrawn during the round (contrast, splash screen, simulation artefacts).

Two things are still unchecked: whether any of the 16 findings round four marked as backlog candidates came back through another path, and whether fix commits in this app after September 11 actually wrote out the six axes.

Checked 2026-11-15. Git history of the P2P chat app repository (commits df1dddc, 684ff8c, 5c44c96, 6c99027, 8f5a0a5, co-authored with Claude Opus 5), the four adversarial review documents (2026-09-08 to 09-11) and the server fix report, the round-four review brief, the project memory for the release-prep round, and commit 6a51d59 in the family scheduling app repository (2026-10-10).

item.title: Daum spell check failed: OkHttp and a JS redirect – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Daum spell check failed: OkHttp and a JS redirect

The page that hands out the key switched to a JavaScript redirect, OkHttp never got the key, and the server answered every check with HTTP 200 and an empty body. Daum was a backup path and nothing counted failures, so no one noticed.

On the night of September 13, 2026, we found that one of the two portal spelling checkers used by SugarSpeller had not succeeded once. The app sends text to two Korean web portals, Naver and Daum (run by Kakao); Naver goes first and Daum is the backup. Daum's server answered every request with HTTP 200 and an empty body.

No one noticed because the app counted the failure nowhere and Daum was not the everyday path. With Daum switched on as the primary checker, the Chat screen would quietly show Naver's result instead. The records do not tell us when it started.

A coloring request led to a 259-byte page

The app has two screens: Chat, the default, where checks go back and forth as message bubbles, and Classic, the older layout with an input box and a result box. That evening the operator asked for the error highlighting to work: it did nothing in Chat and misbehaved in Classic, and both portals' responses should be read properly and turned into colors, Naver first. The working theory was that the response-parsing code was wrong. For Naver it was, and commit e9cd771 fixed that at 20:41 KST.

After the operator said to finish cross-checking Naver and move on, at 22:25 the AI coding agent (Claude Code) fetched the portal page the app loads to get its key. The key here is an authentication value the app must send with every check request. The page body was 259 bytes: a single location.replace() line.

The same check request the app sends then came back with status 200 and a body of size 0. A minute later the agent reported that Daum was "100% dead right now". Having narrowed down the cause, the agent finally checked in the code that the key-fetching function was called. The launch screen called it.

The app sent requests with no valid key

At launch the app downloads the portal's key page, pulls a key out of the HTML, and stores the session cookies set on that response. The page had stopped doing that. It returned one line of JavaScript pointing the browser at a mobile address, with no HTTP 3xx status. OkHttp follows redirects that arrive as a status code plus a Location header; it does not run scripts inside HTML. The app received HTML with no key and no cookies.

When the key was missing, the app carried on. Since commit f11e6e2 on June 12, 2024, the code had held a hard-coded default key, and the app sent checks with it. Daum's server, given a stale key or no session cookie, does not return an error message. It returns 200 and nothing else. The session cookie expires after one day (86,400 seconds), so a key fixed in the code could never pass on its own: the check also needs a fresh cookie from the key page.

Which portal goes first is set by remote config (a Firebase Remote Config value changed without shipping an app update), and the default is Naver. Chat retries once on the other portal when a check fails. With Daum as primary, Chat silently switched to Naver and Classic showed an error toast on every check. When Naver failed and Chat fell back to Daum, the fallback failed too and the user saw an error.

Naver had the same shape. An expired key produced HTTP 200 with an error inside the JSON, the app treated it as a parse exception, and kept failing with the expired key. Commit e9cd771 fixed that the same day by clearing the key and fetching a new one.

Two February changes didn't surface the failure either

On February 26, 2026, two commits co-written with an AI coding agent touched this path. 68c458d replaced the exception with a single "pattern not found" log line and carried on with the existing key. The same day, 6da3f51 added the fallback that retries a failed check on the other portal.

Each change was reasonable, but neither raised a missing key as a failure. After 68c458d that spot became a one-log-line branch, and on September 13 the app went through that branch. With Daum as primary, 6da3f51's fallback covers Daum's failure with Naver's result. We don't know whether the page had already changed in February, or whether Daum was ever switched on as primary through remote config.

There was also no way to see a failure rate. A release-watch note from October 4 says the check failure rate could not be measured, because the success event carried no such value.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Fetching the key from the mobile page, reading an empty body as expiry

Commit 0b74357 (22:44 KST, September 13) stopped trying to follow the redirect and requests the mobile address the script points to. That response carries both the key and the session cookies, and, as the commit message notes, the existing key-extraction code worked on it unchanged.

WhereWhat changedWhat it replaced, and why
Key fetchRequest the mobile address directlySearched the JavaScript page for a key that was never there
Empty bodyTreat it as an expired key: clear it, fetch againTreated as a parse error, so expiry was never visible
Default keyStart emptyA 2024 hard-coded key that masked fetch failures
Returning to the appFetch again if the key is empty, as for NaverFetched only once at launch

The agent also proposed giving Classic the same Naver-to-Daum fallback that day; it was not added and still doesn't exist. Another dead path, a Classic failure branch that called Daum with a different hard-coded key, had already been removed in the Naver commit.

The same commit fixed highlighting as well. To tell requests apart, the app appended an ID string (a short tag per request) to the text it sent, and Daum treated that string as one more word and returned it inside the correction. Replaying 28 saved real-server responses, Daum had flagged 12 errors; the old code colored 6 of them and the new code colors all 12.

The next day a release-only bug blanked Daum's results again. That one is in 203 unit tests missed a release-only blank result: R8 and Gson field names.

Both fixes shipped in version 1.6.017 together with a font fix, described in Android showed some Hangul as blank gaps: NanumSquare's cmap claimed 11,172 syllables but drew only 2,479.

What to check in apps that rely on outside responses

If you keep an unofficial endpoint as a backup, check every day that it still works, separately from user-visible failures.

  1. For each outside API, define success by the body. An empty body, a missing required field or an error field is a failure even with status 200.

  2. If a key or token can't be found in the response that should carry it, fail right there. Don't keep a default key in the code.

  3. Fetch the key page once with an HTTP client that doesn't run scripts (the app's own OkHttp setup, or curl -L). If the body is a single line of script a few hundred bytes long, the app is getting the same thing.

    curl -sL -o body.html -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' <key page URL>

  4. Give the fallback path its own events: the primary failure reason, the fallback attempt and the fallback result.

  5. Save real server responses to files and cross-check parsing and on-screen rendering against them.

Failures are now counted, fallback rescues are not

After a drop in checks could not be explained with the data we had, the October 10 release added a failure event, spell_check_fail. It records which portal failed, why, where the text came from and on which screen. The reason value key covers Naver's error JSON, Daum's 200-with-empty-body and a failed key fetch.

The rule is one event per failure the user actually saw. When Chat's fallback rescues a check, nothing is logged. The success event does record which portal answered, so a Naver failure rescued by Daum shows up as a Daum success. But the state in this incident, Daum dead while Naver works, would still be invisible with today's events.

The September 13 Naver and Daum fixes and the October analytics commit were also co-written with an AI coding agent, and the rule of not counting rescued failures came from that analytics commit.

From October 30 to November 6 there were 20 failures against 4,406 checks, 0.45% across both portals.

A CAPTCHA would break this fix too

The portal does not publish this as an API, so if it changes the page again the same thing can happen. In mid-October the on-device instrumented tests for two versions each had three failures, and the cause was the key page serving a CAPTCHA to the development machine's IP address. When that happens the app gets no key. The code is written so that a failure the user sees then is logged with reason=key, but we have not confirmed that it is actually recorded that way during a CAPTCHA.

Reading an empty body as an expired key rests on what we measured from this one server. A fresh key and cookie returned JSON; a stale key or a missing cookie returned an empty body. An empty body for any other reason will also send the app to fetch a new key. Naver, which reports errors in JSON, needed a different rule.

Next to check: split the failure event by portal, which we have not done yet, to get Daum's failure rate, add a separate event that counts fallback attempts, and decide whether Classic gets a fallback at all.

Checked 2026-11-14. App repository git history (commits f11e6e2, 68c458d, 6da3f51, e9cd771, 0b74357, a611814; the February commits co-written with Claude Opus 4.6, the September ones with Claude Opus 5, the analytics commit with Claude Opus 5.5), the changelog (sections 1.6.017, 1.6.028, 1.6.030, 1.6.031), release-watch notes (October 4, November 7), the Claude Code session log of 2026-09-13 (KST), and the project memory notes on each portal's measured responses (2026-09-13).

item.title: Play Store title keywords: two weeks, no verdict – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Play Store title keywords: two weeks, no verdict

With about one real user a day, changing a Play Store title could not be judged from search ranks alone; the measurement design had to be fixed before the title was.

We rewrote the Google Play title of our Korean document viewer around search keywords, then tracked its search rank for two weeks. On the main keyword, 한글뷰어 ("HWP viewer", also the app's launcher name), it slipped from 13th to 16th, while two other keywords rose. The note we wrote on day 14 says "no clear gain".

The app had about one real user a day, the search page returned a different number of apps each day, and two of the planned measurement days were skipped. Before you change a title, measure a baseline twice with the same script and put the measurement days on a schedule.

Two weeks of ranks

Each run fetched the logged-out Google Play web search page (Korean language, Korea region) with a script and counted where our app sat among the apps on the page. We call the day of the title change, October 18, D0, and count days from there (D+5, D+14). HWP is a Korean word-processor file format, so most of the seven keywords are Korean phrases about opening those files. The new title was "한글뷰어 슈가독: HWP 한글 파일 열기·PDF 저장" in Korean and "SugarDoc HWP Viewer & PDF Save" in English.

Look at the grey bars before the blue dots. The logged-out page returned a different number of apps for the same keyword on different days. For "hwp viewer" it was 22, then 50, then 15. On the day the list grew to 50 our app showed up for the first time, and when the list shrank it was gone again. The October 28 rank file itself put that rank down to the page getting longer.

So the day-14 run on November 1 only compared keywords whose result count (the number of apps the page returned) stayed within one of the previous run.

KeywordOct 28 (D+10)Nov 1 (D+14)Results
한글뷰어 (HWP viewer)14th16th29 → 28
hwp28th20th30 → 29
한글 문서 (HWP document)22nd11th28 → 28
hwp 뷰어 (hwp viewer)25thnot listed50 → 15, not comparable

Two keywords did rise. But the keyword that matches the app's name slipped across both weeks, and 한글 파일 열기 ("open an HWP file"), which went into the title word for word, still did not make an 11-app list. The November 1 rank file calls this "no clear gain" and adds on the next line: "Signal is weak: 1 real user a day".

Four things that blocked a verdict

First, rank was the only thing we could measure. In those two weeks GA4 (Google Analytics 4) counted 0 to 4 real users a day, after filtering out test devices, emulators and Play's pre-launch robots. A rank can move a few places with no way to see whether installs followed. The ASO (app store optimization) plan written the day before the change said there were too few installs for an experiment to mean anything, and that experiments should wait until weekly installs pass 100. The same section also planned rank runs after the title change, and the only conditions attached to the change were shipping and checking the PDF save feature (SAF PDF save: cancelling without empty files).

Second, the list length kept changing, as shown above. Keeping only keywords with a steady result count where our app appeared left the HWP viewer keyword alone on October 28, and three keywords (HWP viewer, hwp, HWP document) on November 1.

Third, the baseline and the later runs did not come from the same script. The "21st before the change" was counted on October 17 from the same logged-out page, fetched with curl for a competitor survey, and inside that same survey the lead agent had counted 20th. The script's first value came five days after the change, at 13th, and the agent that committed it wrote that one run cannot separate the title effect from day-to-day noise.

Fourth, the description, app versions and a help article changed along with the title. The two-week test plan the agent wrote on the day of the change already listed "three things that changed": the store text, the 1.2.0 release with direct PDF save, and a help article on our site. After that the full description changed once more and four more app versions shipped. Play Console's store listing experiments cannot test titles, so there was no control group either.

There was no rank run on October 25, day 7. That morning the operator reported that a landscape slide PDF would not scroll, and that day's five runs went to the daily check, the fix and the 1.3.2 release, and a lock change in the Play upload script. The only measurement days left in the repository are sentences in a rank file note and a commit message. We could not check whether the scheduled runs' instructions included a rank run.

The "keywords in the title get you into the top 10" idea was not confirmed

An agent wrote both the competitor survey and the ASO plan. Its working hypothesis was that a title containing the search words verbatim gets even a small app into the top 5 to 10, based on another app with installs in the hundreds and no ratings that ranked near the top on all seven keywords. The counterexample was already in the same survey: our title contained 한글뷰어 exactly, and we were 21st. Two weeks later, a title containing 한글 파일 열기 verbatim still did not appear for that keyword.

Before the plan was committed, it went through an adversarial check, where a second agent tries to refute each claim. The survey agent had stated "3 real installs" as fact; the check changed that to "public install band 1+, 2 to 3 daily users in the console" and marked the cause of the low rank as a guess.

On October 8 the operator read a trademark search and chose to use 한글뷰어 in the title. On the day the new title was uploaded to Play at 15:45 Korea time, the agent listed a two-week Google Ads test as the next step. When the operator asked whether a 14-day spend was really needed, the agent withdrew the advice, saying that with ads running at the same time a rise in installs could not be traced to the title or the ads. The operator then decided not to spend money, to publish search articles instead, and to plan ads after the two-week test. No record shows a person changing the measurement design.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Five days of checking a stale copy

The desk that prepares these notes missed the result too. The day-14 file was already on the remote main on November 1, but our harness, the scheduled script that runs agents to check story ideas, only looked at the local copy and postponed this post on November 2 and 6 as "not measured yet". The November 6 morning check even missed the October 23 and 28 files that were already in that copy. The copy was behind the remote; the run early on November 7 read the remote directly with git show origin/main:<path>, found the file, and added the same rule to the desk's procedure.

Users rose after day 14

After the verdict, daily real users went up: 5 on November 3, 11 on November 9.

We cannot tie this to the title. In the same weeks, short video posts started, tablet screenshots went up on the store listing, and the site moved to a new address. The backlog said "next rank check November 8", and that run never happened.

If your app has single-digit daily users, do not judge a store title change by search rank. Until weekly installs pass 100, log it and stop there.

This comes from one app, seven keywords and four runs. We never measured twice on the same day to see how many places the rank wobbles on its own, and we did not record whether competing apps changed their titles in those two weeks. Measurements from the viewer engine side of the same app are in Building an Android HWP viewer with rhwp: measured. The plan to alternate the title with a spaced spelling, 한글 뷰어, has not started.

These are the measurements we did not use this time.

MethodWhy not this timeWhen it fits
Search installs in Play Console's store listing acquisition reportThe ASO plan left it to the operator, and nobody opened it this timeOnce installs pile up enough to count search traffic on its own
Rank on a real, logged-in phonePlanned as "once on the same day", but no record existsWhen you need to know how far the logged-out web order is from what users see
A Console experiment on the short descriptionTitles cannot be tested, and the plan judged installs too few to mean anythingAfter weekly installs pass 100

What to pin down before the next title change

  1. Measure the baseline at least twice with the same script you will use afterwards. Fetch https://play.google.com/store/search?q=<keyword>&c=apps&hl=ko&gl=KR, list the distinct app ids in the order they appear on the page, and use your app's position in that list as its rank.

  2. Record the result count (the number of distinct app ids) next to every rank, and compare only keywords whose count stays within one. Keep the rest as "not comparable". One line per keyword and day is enough.

    date | keyword | rank | results | changed that day
2026-11-01 | 한글뷰어 | 16 | 28 | nothing

  3. Put the measurement days on a schedule, including a run on the day of the change (D0).

  4. Change the title and nothing else. If a description, app version, help article or screenshot changes in the window, write it in the last column.

  5. Write the verdict rule into the repository first. Following the logic of the November 1 verdict, call it a gain only if the main keyword rose on a like-for-like basis at both D+7 and D+14.

  6. Read measurement files from the remote with git show origin/main:<path>. Our local copy was more than two weeks behind.

Checked 2026-11-13. The app repository's three rank files (1cc0044, 68215b5, 9043d19), weekly_rank.py, the competitor survey and ASO plan (8475f45), store text changes (c4f1dd3, 1b7c328), GA4 real-user values in the daily ops reports (Oct 27 to Nov 11), the run log, Claude Code session transcripts from Oct 17 and 18, and this desk's check records (Nov 2 to 7; the local copy was 28 changes behind).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.description:
AX notes · Retrospective

Flutter vs native solo dev: one studio, two picks

The stack followed where each app does its work and how many platforms reuse the same screens; the family app's Flutter choice was accepted only as a two-week spike with exit rules.

In September 2026, SugarMount decided to build its Android utility portfolio in Kotlin, and 15 days later to build a family scheduling app in Flutter. Both decisions were written down with their reasons, so it is possible to see what split them.

The split came down to whether an app's work is concentrated in platform features such as video transcoding, widgets and special permissions or in screens and domain logic, and to how many platforms will run the same screens. An AI agent's research for the family app also produced a person-day comparison; a second agent flagged the same day that its premise and its math disagreed, and recomputing shows the "about the same" verdict rested on an assumption the document never stated.

The utility apps went Kotlin because of platform features

The utility repository's first architecture decision record (ADR, a short file explaining why a choice was made), ADR-0001, was accepted by the operator the day the repository was created. It chose Kotlin, Jetpack Compose and Material 3 for the portfolio (19 apps at the time, trimmed to 14 the next day), one module per app in a single repository, and left iOS undecided.

The first reason was where the cost lives. These apps do their real work in the platform layer: video transcoding with Media3 Transformer, MediaStore, home screen widgets, special permissions. A cross-platform UI layer would save little, because those engines would still be written once per platform. The second reason was iOS. App Store Review Guideline 4.3(a) forbids shipping the same app under multiple bundle IDs, and a family of near-identical utility apps is a Play Store strategy. Setting a ringtone or keeping the screen on while another app runs cannot be done on iOS at all. The record also cites an earlier attempt to port the studio's Korean spell-checker app to Flutter: the UI reached 99.8% and the port stalled at ads, billing and MP4 encoding, never shipping.

iOS was not ruled out for good. Some shared modules avoid importing Android packages so the top one or two apps could later move to Kotlin Multiplatform (sharing Kotlin code across platforms). The decision is to be revisited once five apps are live and there is revenue data, an Apple developer account and a Mac build path.

The family app needed the same screens three times

The family app was planned for Android and a desktop web app first, iOS later. Family members carry different phones, so the same calendar and photo screens have to exist on all three. The agent's stack research compared four options.

OptionVerdictDeciding reason
React Native / ExpoRejectedNot on the official platform list for AdMob (Google's mobile ads); device attestation for Firebase App Check (the app integrity check) must be hand-built; no prior experience
FlutterChosen, conditional on spikesAI, ads and billing SDKs all official; screens written once; about 33,700 lines of prior Dart experience
Kotlin Android + Next.js webFallbackBest Android quality and code reuse, but every feature built twice, three times with iOS
Kotlin / Compose MultiplatformRejectedNo official Firebase SDK; web target still in Beta

Both rejected options hit a gap in official SDK support: AdMob for React Native, Firebase for Kotlin/Compose Multiplatform.

The research also named what Flutter gave up: the utility repository's Kotlin modules for ads, billing, WebP encoding and share handling could not be reused as is, only ported piece by piece through Kotlin platform channels (the bridge Flutter code uses to call native Android code).

The AI estimate's premise and its math disagreed

Section 4 of the research estimated solo maintenance cost in person-days for V0, the first release: 12 Android screens and 6 web screens. Its premise priced one screen at 1.5 person-days on both Android and web, but the table priced only Flutter's web screens at half that, 0.75 days. That is how the totals came out at 27.5 versus 28, "about the same."

A separate agent reviewed the document adversarially that day. Row A7 of its findings called this an "internal inconsistency." Below are part of the table and the A7 row, rendered in English from the Korean original.

The reviewer did not say 0.75 was wrong. If code sharing makes Flutter web screens cheaper, it said, write that into the premise. Apply the stated 1.5 days to Flutter's web screens as well and Flutter's V0 total becomes 32 person-days, so for Android and web alone the Kotlin route comes out cheaper. With estimates that have no data behind them, a gap this small should not pick the stack.

The review section opens with "the body was not edited," and the decision record written the same day, ADR-07, repeated those totals. ADR-07 accepted the other point (A6, iOS cost underestimated) and revised the with-iOS figure to roughly 36 to 38 versus roughly 57 person-days (estimates). The reasons the decision record left are the iOS gap, the official SDKs and the operator's Flutter experience.

The research's opening argument got corrected too. Using planning-stage subscription assumptions, it claimed the condition for launching on iOS would be "met almost immediately," and used that to argue for Flutter. Review finding A4 called that an overstatement. The operator's own rule was to ship iOS only after income "comfortably" exceeds Apple's fee, and that fee alone would take more than half of the operator's monthly fixed-cost cap of 20,000 won (about $14). The decision records moved iOS behind a separate gate whose thresholds the operator sets.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The decision was a two-week spike with exit rules

ADR-07's status column reads "recommended (presumed accepted)," and the same file defines that as a recommendation the operator did not object to. Flutter was not locked in; it was adopted on condition that six risky paths be checked within two weeks. The research wrote the condition and each spike's (a short build to test one risk) pass bar and fallback in advance; ADR-07 carried over the spike list and the exit rule.

SpikeWhat it had to proveIf it failed
S1Receiving shared files: app not running, signed out, many images, PDFNative Kotlin channel; if still failing, Kotlin + web
S2A 1080×2400 screenshot to a readable 20 KB WebP in under 1 sDifferent web encoder, shrink on device
S3AI extraction call with App Check enforcedKotlin + web
S4AdMob Next-Gen (the newer version of Google's ads SDK) banner and consent flow in an R8 build (the tool that shrinks and renames code in Android release builds), plus a monkey testPort the existing Kotlin ad module
S5Local reminders across reboot, Doze, denied exact-alarm permissionKotlin channel
S6Flutter web first load, drag-and-drop upload, KakaoTalk in-app browserSplit only the web to Next.js

The exit rule is also stated as a count: if two or more of S1, S3 and S4 cannot be solved in Flutter, switch to Kotlin Android plus a separate web app; if only S6 fails, split off just the web.

The Next-Gen ads SDK hit the same R8 crash as 16 days earlier

The first spike build ran on October 8 as an R8 release build on an API 35 emulator. S1 passed: shares arrived at the review screen in all four cases. That share handling was written as a Kotlin platform channel, without a Flutter plugin.

S2 passed only for photos. All 10 synthetic photos fit under 20,480 bytes, but four of five dense synthetic school notices stayed slightly over target even at 800 px and quality 20. This is the device screen from that run.

S2 was not part of the exit rule, so it did not affect the stack verdict. The agent listed three options and recommended allowing documents alone up to a hard cap of 24,576 bytes, but because that changes a product requirement, it left the call to the operator.

S4 was only half checked that day. The installed Flutter 3.35.1 could only use the ad plugin's Legacy path (the older version of the SDK), which survived two 3,000-event monkey runs with zero crashes. The app would ship on Next-Gen, so that result could not close S4. Testing Next-Gen meant upgrading Flutter, a global install, so the agent stopped and noted that it needed the operator's consent.

The next day, after moving to Flutter 3.47.7 and switching on Next-Gen, the release build on a Galaxy S21 crashed at launch, three times in a row. The Next-Gen SDK pulls in an old version of Room (an on-device database library) through WorkManager (a background job library). That Room version's keep rule (a rule naming code R8 must not remove) protects database classes but not their constructors.

R8 full mode (the more aggressive shrinking mode) used that gap to strip the constructor of WorkManager's database, and WorkManager failed during startup. The family app fixed it with this one line:

-keep class * extends androidx.room.RoomDatabase { void <init>(); }

The utility apps had hit the same crash 16 days earlier. On September 23 a utility release died at launch for the same reason, and the same kind of rule went into the shared ad module (AI-built Android app release checklist: R8 crash covers that release). The family app's spike report and its rule file comment never mention the earlier fix. When you start a new stack, bring over your previous project's keep rules first. Another Next-Gen crash is in GMA Next-Gen ad callbacks run off the main thread.

With that fix and a corrected initialization order, S4 passed with zero crashes in a 2,000-event monkey run on the S21. By October 9, S1 and S4 had both passed, so the exit rule could no longer trigger.

Not for content pages or look-alike app portfolios

Even the family app did not build its whole web presence in Flutter. The research noted that Flutter web ships as a heavy single-page app and that Flutter's own docs advise against it for content sites, so only the signed-in app uses Flutter web; the landing and invite pages are static HTML, partly because invite links open inside KakaoTalk's in-app browser (KakaoTalk is Korea's most widely used messenger).

For a portfolio of near-identical apps, App Store rule 4.3 erases Flutter's main advantage, sharing code with iOS. Without prior Flutter experience, one of the family app's reasons disappears entirely.

S3's App Check part, S5 and S6 still have no verdict

We found no recorded result for S6 (Flutter web) in the family app repository. For S5 (local reminders), the notification feature was built and merged on October 10, but there is no verdict against the S5 bar (reboot, Doze, within one minute of the scheduled time). S3 has a measurement report comparing AI extraction models, and the decision record gained a model and prompt decision made on the operator's instruction, but there is no verdict anywhere on running with App Check enforced.

The October 5 backlog says spike verdicts go into an ADR-07 update; S5 and S6 are not there yet.

As of November 13, 2026.
